chapter_theme: Manimekala, disguised as a townswoman, sends Sudhamathi and Manimekalai into the Chakravala Kottam beside Puhar's burning ground and explains its name: she describes the cemetery that teaches death spares no one, and tells how the Brahmin boy Sarngalan died of fright there, how the goddess Champapathi told his mother Gotami that his own deed and not a demon took him, refused her life in exchange, and had every god of the cosmos confirm that none can give back a life; on that spot Maya modelled the whole world-system. Then the goddess carries the sleeping girl to Manipallavam.

cast.role: the sea goddess, Kovalan's family deity, who tells the tale of the shrine and carries Manimekalai to Manipallavam
Manimekalai's companion, who hears the tale and falls asleep
Madhavi's daughter, carried off asleep to Manipallavam
the old ascetic goddess of the city, guardian of the burning ground, called here சம்பாபதி and முது மூதாட்டி
a Brahmin woman of Puhar with a blind husband, Sarngalan's mother
Gotami's young son, a Brahmin youth who dies of fright in the burning ground
the demon woman who eats a corpse's eyes and dances in the burning ground
Death, called the worker of the cruel trade
the gods of every rank in the Chakravala, gathered by Champapathi
the divine builder who models the cosmos in clay

manimekalai:6:1-15.reading: After the evening has passed the moon rises, its spot showing in the clear sky as a fault shows plainly in the worthy, pouring light over the grove like milk from a silver pot; the goddess Manimekala, a body bright as lightning given form, bows and praises the seat of the first lord who turns the wheel of dharma, takes the shape of a woman of the town and asks Sudhamathi why they are standing there.
manimekalai:6:1-15.nuance: The simile at lines 3 to 5 runs the Kural's comparison backwards: the couplet compares the fault of the high-born to the moon's spot, and here the moon's spot is compared to the fault of the worthy, as if the moral were the better-known term. The lord of the wheel of dharma whose foot-seat she worships (11 to 12) is the Buddha by the epic's usage; the unit does not name him.
manimekalai:6:1-15.event: Manimekala comes to the grove at moonrise, worships at the Buddha's seat and, disguised as a townswoman, asks Sudhamathi why she stands there.

claims.claim: a fault in the worthy shows as plainly as the spot on the moon

manimekalai:6:16-33.reading: When Sudhamathi tells what the prince said, the goddess warns that he has not given up his gaze on the girl and, though he left calling the grove the ascetics' wood, will keep haunting the outer streets, so they should leave by the small western gate into the Chakravala Kottam, where great ascetics live, and come to no harm though the night passes; Sudhamathi answers that apart from the trickster vidyadhara Maruthavegan and the goddess herself everyone in the city calls the place only the cremation-ground shrine, and asks why she gives it another name.
manimekalai:6:16-33.nuance: The goddess judges that Sudhamathi's sermon in the previous kaathai has not worked: the prince's look is unabated (தணியா நோக்கம்), and the answer now is refuge in place rather than argument. Sudhamathi's question sets up the whole kaathai as an explanation of a name: what the city calls the burning ground's shrine, the goddess calls by the name of the cosmos.
manimekalai:6:16-33.event: The goddess tells Sudhamathi to take Manimekalai by the west gate into the Chakravala Kottam; Sudhamathi asks why it bears that name when the city calls it the burning-ground shrine.
manimekalai:6:16-33.unit_note: Boundary moved from 31|32 to 33|34: Sudhamathi's question begun at line 27 runs to ஈங்கு இதன் காரணம் என்னையோ? என at line 33; line 34 (ஆங்கு அதன் காரணம் அறியக் கூறுவன்) begins the goddess's answer.

manimekalai:6:34-47.reading: The goddess says she will tell the reason, even if deep night comes upon Madhavi's daughter, and begins: beside this place lies the cremation ground that arose with the famous city itself, with four gates, one painted with a chariot that is never driven where the gods enter, one painted with paddy, cane, water and groves, one of plain white plaster with no figure inside, and one where a tall clay figure stands with folded red lips, fierce eyes, noose and trident.
manimekalai:6:34-47.nuance: The cemetery is as old as the city (37 to 38): the city of festivals in the earlier kaathais and the place of the dead are founded together. The fourth gate's figure with noose and trident reads as Death's guardian, though the unit does not name him.
manimekalai:6:34-47.event: The goddess begins to explain the shrine's name by describing the four gates of the old cremation ground beside it.
manimekalai:6:34-47.unit_note: Starts at line 34 after the boundary moved from 31|32 to 33|34 (see manimekalai:6:16-33); the end at 47 is unchanged.

manimekalai:6:48-63.reading: Within the guarded wall stand the great shrine of the goddess who dwells in the forest, where the heads of those who with unwavering heart paid life's debt hang from a tall tree; tall shrines of burnt brick, short and high like hills, raised by the eminent for the dead, whether ascetics, kings or women who died together with their husbands, kept apart by the four varnas; altars of offering to fierce gods, stone platforms, and the huts where guards with staff and skull-bowl eat and sleep.
manimekalai:6:48-63.nuance: The cemetery keeps distinctions the dead no longer have: memorials are sorted by varna (56), and ascetics, kings and women who died with their husbands each get their own. The heads hung at the forest goddess's shrine (50 to 51) are of those who offered their own lives; the goddess describes them without comment here, but her account later (164 to 166) bears on what such offerings achieve. Taking உயிர்க் கடன் இறுத்தோர் (50) as those who offered their own heads is the plain sense, not a certain one.

manimekalai:6:64-77.reading: Smoke-flags, flaming arches and funeral pandals are everywhere; those who burn, who lay out, who put in dug pits, who shut in vaults and who cover with urns come and go night and day without pause; the dirge drum that shakes the heart, the cry of worship when an ascetic dies and the wailing when others die, the jackal's howl, the owl that calls the dying, and the cries of the flesh-eating kural and the horned owl fill it.
manimekalai:6:64-77.nuance: Lines 66 and 67 list five ways of disposing of the dead side by side, burning, exposure, pit burial, vault and urn, with no one way set above another. Lines 72 and 73 set the ascetic's death, greeted with worship, against the ordinary death, greeted with weeping: the only difference the cemetery records between the renouncer and the rest.

manimekalai:6:78-93.reading: An unpleasant noise like the roar of the sea never ceases there; thanri, oduvai and ulinjil trees rise and thorn and cactus crowd, bands of starving demons gather, and there are the halls under the vaagai, the vilam where birds feast on fat, the vanni where the cremation-ground vow-keepers light fires with steady hearts, the iratthi where those vowed in body gather skulls, and the open hall where corpse-eaters feast from pots of fat, with fire pots, skull-bowls, bier poles and shrouds lying about.
manimekalai:6:78-93.nuance: The ascetics of the burning ground, the சுடலை நோன்பிகள் and விரத யாக்கையர், are listed among the cemetery's sights beside the corpse-eaters, not apart from them; the Buddhist goddess describes them without praise.

manimekalai:6:94-104.reading: Over the wide field lie torn garlands, broken pots, paddy, puffed rice and grains of offering; and the goddess asks whether, seeing the cruel worker Death kill and heap up ascetics, the very rich, young mothers just delivered, helpless infants, old and young without distinction, for this fiery burning ground to eat, there can be greater fools than people who revel in wealth and drink and live without desiring dharma.
manimekalai:6:94-104.nuance: The list of the dead (97 to 99) puts the ascetic first and the infant beside the rich man: tapas, wealth and youth buy no exemption. The conclusion is aram, not fame or giving; the next unit tells of one who saw the same sights and died of them.

claims.claim: death takes ascetic and rich, infant and old alike
those who see the burning ground and still live revelling in wealth and drink without desiring dharma are the greatest fools

manimekalai:6:105-131.reading: A Brahmin youth named Sarngalan, going alone and taking the place for a guarded city, comes among sights that proclaim to the attached that the body is bone, flesh and blood: a jackal howling with a lac-dyed foot torn from a worm-ridden lump, a vulture tearing the girdled hips, a dog crunching a braceleted hand, a starving vulture eating sandal-smeared breasts, and a demon woman who lifts a dark head on the ash-white stage, scoops out and eats its eyes without stopping to ask whether hair or cloud, eye or carp, lip or flower, tooth or pearl, and dances; terrified, he flees crying to his mother that he has given his life to the old demon of the burning ground, falls before her and lays down his body.
manimekalai:6:105-131.nuance: The demon woman's 'cloud or hair? carp or eye?' (122 to 124) is the lover's comparison of love poetry taken apart limb by limb: what the poems doubt between, she eats without asking. The parts eaten are the parts a lover praises: dyed foot, girdled hips, braceleted hand, sandal-smeared breast. Who 'proclaims' at 107 to 108 is not plain; the sights are read here as the subject. The boy sees exactly what is meant to teach detachment and dies of fear.
manimekalai:6:105-131.event: Sarngalan wanders into the burning ground at night, sees a demon woman eating a corpse's eyes and dancing, runs home in terror, and dies before his mother.

claims.claim: the body is bone, flesh and blood

manimekalai:6:105-131.unit_note: Boundary moved from 122|123 to 131|132, merging the old units 105-122 and 123-135 up to line 131: the demon woman's dance begun at 118 runs into line 126, and Sarngalan's flight and death close at 131 (மெய் வைத்தலும்); line 132 begins his mother's lament.

manimekalai:6:132-153.reading: His mother Gotami, a woman who lives with a blind Brahmin and has no one else, clasps her son's body at the burning ground's outer gate and cries to Champapathi, guardian of the ghats, halls, old trees, dwellings and shrines, asking whether a demon or a spirit has eaten his life and whether she has no justice; the golden goddess appears asking why she is called at midnight, hears that the helpless boy lies as if asleep, and answers that neither spirits nor demons eat lives: with the Brahmin boy's terror as its occasion, his own former deed came, ate his life and went, so she should give up her grief.
manimekalai:6:132-153.nuance: Champapathi denies that a spirit or demon kills and gives the deed (ஊழ்வினை) as the cause, with fright only as its occasion (பேது கந்தாக, 151): the cemetery's demon, so vivid in the previous unit, is reduced to an occasion. Gotami's word for herself, தீத்தொழிலாட்டியேன் (133), blames her own past deeds before the goddess does.
manimekalai:6:132-153.event: Gotami carries her dead son to the burning-ground gate and calls on Champapathi, who appears and tells her that his former deed, not a demon, took his life.

claims.claim: spirits and demons do not take a life; a former deed ripens and takes it, with fright only as its occasion

manimekalai:6:132-153.unit_note: Starts at line 132 after the boundary moved from 122|123 to 131|132 (see manimekalai:6:105-131); ends at line 153, where Champapathi's first answer closes (என்றலும்), instead of 159; lines 154 to 159 begin Gotami's offer and the goddess's reply, which runs to 167.

manimekalai:6:154-167.reading: Gotami begs the goddess to take her life and give back his, so that he may look after her blind husband; the old goddess, pitying her, answers that once a life has gone it surely goes by its deeds into another birth, that bringing it back is not in her power, that the offer is like the false and wretched saying of those whose trade holds that killing is dharma, and asks whether there have not been those who gave their lives for the world's kings, and yet in this burning ground stand a thousand shrines for kings; she bids her leave such hell-bound words.
manimekalai:6:154-167.nuance: Champapathi counts a mother's offer of her own life in exchange as killing, and so as the same error as the claim that killing is dharma (162 to 163); 'those whose trade' it is are not named, and the unit does not say whether sacrificers or others are meant. Lines 164 to 166 answer the offer from the cemetery itself: lives given for kings did not keep the kings alive. Reading 164 as 'give their lives in place of the kings' lives' is the plainer sense but not certain.
manimekalai:6:154-167.event: Gotami offers her life for her son's; Champapathi refuses, saying a departed life goes on by its deeds and that a life given for another saves no one.

claims.claim: once a life departs it goes to a new birth according to the deeds done
the saying that killing is dharma is a false and wretched word
a life given in place of another's does not keep that other alive

manimekalai:6:154-167.unit_note: Starts at line 154 after the boundary moved from 159|160 to 153|154 and ends at 167 (என்றலும்), where Champapathi's reply closes, instead of 175; line 168 begins Gotami's appeal to the Brahmins' books.

manimekalai:6:168-187.reading: Gotami says that the Brahmins of the four Vedas declare in their books that the gods grant boons, and that if the great goddess will not grant one she will not keep her own life; Champapathi answers that unless the first one of the aeon gives life, if those who move within the ring of the world can give it she will too, and to show her power she sets before Gotami all who can grant boons in the Chakravala, the four classes of formless Brahmas, the sixteen of Brahmas with form, the two lights, the six kinds of gods, the many asuras, the eight kinds of beings in hell, the stars and planets, and asks them to end her sorrow, and every god there says just what Champapathi said.
manimekalai:6:168-187.nuance: Gotami's appeal to the Veda's promise of boons is answered by assembling every god of the cosmos to deny it; the gods here are beings within the world-system, not above it. The ranks named, formless and form Brahmas in four and sixteen kinds within a Chakravala, are the Buddhist cosmology, which is the ground for tagging the claim Buddhist. Who 'the first one of the aeon' (172) is, whose giving Champapathi excepts, the unit does not say.
manimekalai:6:168-187.event: Gotami cites the Vedas' promise of boons; Champapathi summons every boon-giving god of the Chakravala, and all confirm that none can give back the boy's life.

claims.claim: the gods grant boons to those who ask
no being within the world-system, god or Brahma, can give back a departed life

manimekalai:6:168-187.unit_note: Starts at line 168 after the boundary moved from 159|160 to 153|154 and from 175|176 to 167|168; the end at 187 is unchanged.

manimekalai:6:188-205.reading: Her grief gone, Gotami places her son in the burning ground and dies; then, to show Champapathi's power, in the place where all the gods had gathered the great Maya modelled in clay the ring-mountain bounded by the sea, Meru standing at the centre, the seven ranges around it, the four great continents, the two thousand small islands and all their regions, with the beings that live in each, so that the order of things could be known; this is the Chakravala Kottam, and because it lies outside the wall of the shrine of the dead, people call it only the cremation-ground shrine; that, says the goddess, is its origin.
manimekalai:6:188-205.nuance: Gotami's grief ends because the gods' confession convinced her, and she dies of her own accord (189): the tale does not call it suicide or praise it. The cosmos model stands on the spot where every god admitted he could not undo a death, so the shrine teaches the order of the world from the place of that admission; the name the city uses forgets it.
manimekalai:6:188-205.event: Gotami lays her son in the burning ground and dies; Maya models the whole cosmos in clay on the gods' meeting place, and this becomes the Chakravala Kottam.
manimekalai:6:188-205.unit_note: Boundary moved from 199|200 to 205|206: the description of the model runs from line 192 through காண் at 202 to the goddess's closing words at 205 (இதன் வரவு இது' என்று இருந் தெய்வம் உரைக்க); lines 206 to 214 turn back to Sudhamathi and Manimekalai.

manimekalai:6:206-214.reading: As the goddess tells of the life of those who are born, Sudhamathi, her simple heart overcome by sorrow, falls asleep in the deep midnight; the goddess embraces Manimekalai, carries her thirty yojanas south through the sky to Manipallavam, girded by waves, sets her down there and departs.
manimekalai:6:206-214.nuance: The goddess's story of Gotami is called the life of those who are born (பிறந்தோர் வாழ்க்கை, 207), a summary of birth itself; it puts Sudhamathi to sleep and leaves Manimekalai to wake alone on the island of her former births.
manimekalai:6:206-214.event: Sudhamathi falls asleep, and the goddess carries Manimekalai through the sky to Manipallavam and leaves her there.
manimekalai:6:206-214.unit_note: Starts at line 206 after the boundary moved from 199|200 to 205|206 (see manimekalai:6:188-205).

links.note: The couplet says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; the epic's moonrise says the moon's spot shows like a fault in the worthy.
links.teaches: The epic can use the couplet's moral as the familiar term of a comparison for the sky, which shows the saying was common enough to be turned round.

gains.a: The odd simile of a moon's spot shown like a worthy man's fault gets its source and its direction.
gains.b: The couplet is seen working as a known saying that a narrative poet could invert in passing.

links.note: Sudhamathi's sermon on the body did not reach the prince before the sight of the girl; here the goddess reports that his gaze has not abated and sends the women into refuge.
links.teaches: The epic marks the failure of the sermon on the body as a fact the plot acts on: after argument fails, protection becomes a matter of place and then of flight.

links.note: Madhavi ranks first among pathini women those who give up their lives when their husbands die; the cemetery holds brick shrines for women who died together with their husbands, sorted by varna beside ascetics and kings.
links.teaches: The death Madhavi praises as the highest kind of chastity ends, in the goddess's tour, as one more class of memorial in a field whose lesson is that no death is exempt.

links.note: The Purananuru poem describes the same burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and dancing demon women, which has taken even conquerors, and urges the patron to give freely and win lasting fame; the goddess draws from it that revelling in wealth instead of desiring dharma is the height of folly.
links.teaches: The same memento mori leads the puram poet to gift and fame that outlast the body, and the Buddhist epic to dharma, with no word of fame: the cemetery's lesson changes with what each tradition thinks survives.

gains.a: The goddess's verdict is seen to drop the fame and the patron that the older use of the scene required.
gains.b: The poem's turn from the burning ground to fame is shown to be a choice, since the same scene could argue for renunciation.

links.note: The quatrain's speaker, having seen teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground, will not listen to talk of teeth like pearls; the demon woman eats the eyes without asking 'tooth or pearl', and Sarngalan, seeing it, dies of fright.
links.teaches: The sight of the burning ground that steadies the Naladiyar's renouncer kills an unready boy, so the contemplation of the dead body is shown to need a prepared mind and not merely a sight.

gains.a: Sarngalan's death is read as a failed contemplation of the body, not only a ghost story.
gains.b: The quatrain's confident resolve gets a counter-case in which the same evidence destroys the one who sees it.

links.note: The quatrain warns that merciless Death stalks and takes even the child while its mother wails; Gotami wails over her son and asks whether a spirit took him, and Champapathi answers that no spirit takes a life, only the boy's former deed.
links.teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's wailing mother a voice and an answer, and the answer removes the stalking agent the quatrain imagines: what takes the child is his own deed, with fright as its occasion.

gains.a: Champapathi's denial of a killing agent stands out against the ethics book's ready personification of Death.
gains.b: The quatrain's figure of Death as a thief is shown to be one account among others, which a Buddhist epic replaces with karma.

links.note: The couplet sets not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; Champapathi calls 'killing is dharma' a false word and counts a mother's offer of her own life for her son's under it.
links.teaches: The epic extends the couplet's rule against killing to giving one's own life in exchange for another's, which the couplet, concerned with animals and sacrifice, does not consider.

gains.a: Champapathi's sharp refusal of a mother's offer is seen to rest on the ethics of not killing, not on want of pity.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is carried to the case of self-offering, where its scope is tested by a sympathetic petitioner.

links.note: In Puhar's festival warriors set their own heads on the altar praying that the offering be a bulwark of the king's strength, and the narrator does not judge it; Champapathi says lives have been given for kings, yet the burning ground holds a thousand kings' shrines.
links.teaches: On the plainer reading of lines 164 to 166, the second epic denies what the first epic's rite assumes, that a life given for the king protects him, and it does so in the same city.

links.note: Maalathi carries a Brahmin household's dead baby to every shrine, Saathan says the gods give no boon to those without tapas yet hands her a child by becoming it; Gotami, a Brahmin's wife with a dead son, appeals to the gods' boons and every god of the Chakravala says none can give back a life.
links.teaches: The two epics tell the same story of a grieving mother at Puhar's shrines with opposite endings: a god supplies a living child by illusion in one, while in the other the gods together refuse even that, and the mother dies.

links.note: The couplet says that for those who have gained the power of tapas even leaping past Death becomes possible; Champapathi, the old ascetic goddess, shows her power by proving that no god can give back a life.
links.teaches: The power over death that tapas earns, in the epic, stops at the one who earned it: even the oldest ascetic goddess and all the gods cannot pass it to the dead.

gains.a: Champapathi's display of power is seen as a demonstration of a limit, not a failure of her tapas.
gains.b: The couplet's 'even' is given a firm boundary: tapas may carry one past death but cannot bring another back.

new_concepts.gloss: the world-system of Buddhist cosmology: a ring of mountains enclosing Meru, the continents, the heavens and the hells with all their beings
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: சக்கரவாளக் கோட்டம் (24, 31, 202), சக்கரவாளத்து (183)

source_issues: Line 71: a leftover HTML quote mark at the start of the line was removed by the build (show's repair flag).

Lines 34 to 36: the goddess's answer opens with a quotation mark placed mid-line before இந், after நேர் இழை கூறும், and her speech, which contains the quoted speeches of Gotami and Champapathi, closes only at line 205 (இதன் வரவு இது'); the nested quotations at 128 to 130 and 132 to 138 use double marks inside it.
Line 214 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.
Line 172: ஊழி முதல்வன், whose giving of life Champapathi excepts, is not identified in the unit; the sense of lines 172 to 174 is uncertain.
